\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Model Collapse in Iterative Training}

\citet{shumailov2024ai} demonstrate that language models trained recursively on their own generated data undergo irreversible tail distribution erosion, establishing model collapse as a fundamental limitation of self-consuming training loops. \citet{dohmatob2024tale} further analyze this through scaling laws, showing that synthetic data truncates heavy-tailed input distributions, causing loss of scaling and skill degradation---directly relevant to the rare n-gram tail erosion we observe. \citet{alemohammad2024self} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD), proving theoretically that without fresh real data, iterative self-consumption degrades either quality or diversity. Subsequent work has extended these findings along several axes: \citet{dohmatob2025strong} establish a sharp phase transition in collapse behavior beyond a critical iteration threshold; \citet{seddik2024how} derive the maximum synthetic data proportion before collapse becomes inevitable; and \citet{guo2024curious} track the decay of lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity across self-training generations, finding the strongest degradation in high-entropy generation tasks.

On the mitigation side, \citet{gerstgrasser2024model} show that accumulating data across generations---rather than replacing it---can prevent collapse, while \citet{briesch2023large} confirm that replacement-based training degrades output diversity proportionally to synthetic data fraction. Our work operates within the replacement setting where collapse is expected, but reveals that a natural mitigation strategy---diversity-based data selection---can paradoxically \emph{accelerate} rather than prevent collapse when it relies on the training model's own representations.

It is instructive to contrast self-consuming language model training with self-play in reinforcement learning \citep{silver2017mastering} and self-training with verification \citep{singh2024beyond}. In both settings, models train iteratively on their own outputs, yet collapse does not occur---because an external reward signal (game outcome, unit test, verifier) anchors the training distribution. Pure language model self-training lacks such an anchor: the model is both generator and (implicit) evaluator, and embedding-based selection provides a proxy signal that degrades endogenously rather than an external ground truth that remains stable.

\subsection{Data Curation and Selection for LLM Training}

Data selection has emerged as a key lever for training efficiency and quality. \citet{sorscher2022beyond} show that metric-guided data pruning can break neural scaling law power laws, motivating a family of embedding-based and model-aware selection methods. SemDeDup \citep{abbas2023semdedup} removes semantic near-duplicates using pretrained embeddings; D4 \citep{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversity-maximizing selection in embedding space; and DSIR \citep{xie2023data} selects data via importance resampling to match target domain feature distributions. More recent approaches optimize for task-specific signals: LESS \citep{xia2024less} selects instruction-tuning data based on gradient similarity to target tasks; DsDm \citep{engstrom2024dsdm} frames selection as datamodel-based optimization, noting that naive quality proxies can harm downstream performance; QuRating \citep{wettig2024qurating} uses LLM-generated quality scores; and SelectIT \citep{liu2024selectit} leverages model uncertainty for instruction data filtering.

These methods are designed for one-shot curation of static datasets, where the embedding model is fixed and its representation quality is not in question. We show that the iterative self-training setting introduces a qualitatively different failure mode: when the model providing embeddings co-degrades with the training distribution, embedding-based selection amplifies rather than counteracts distributional collapse. Data mixing strategies that blend real and synthetic data across generations \citep{gerstgrasser2024model} offer a complementary mitigation but do not address the selection mechanism itself.

\subsection{Embedding-Based Diversity and Representation Learning}

Submodular maximization provides the algorithmic foundation for embedding-based diversity selection. \citet{iyer2013submodular} establish the optimization framework for submodular functions under budget constraints; \citet{wei2015submodularity} formalize data subset selection via facility location and graph-cut objectives in feature space; and \citet{mirzasoleiman2020coresets} apply gradient-embedding facility location for coreset construction. These methods assume a fixed, high-quality embedding space---an assumption we show breaks down under iterative self-training.

Active learning methods face a related challenge: acquisition functions must remain well-calibrated as the model updates. BADGE \citep{ash2020deep} selects diverse batches via gradient embeddings; BatchBALD \citep{kirsch2019batchbald} maximizes joint mutual information; and subsequent work has shown that standard acquisition strategies degrade under distribution shift \citep{kothawade2021similar} and that embedding quality determines selection effectiveness \citep{yehuda2022active}. However, active learning typically involves a few rounds of model updating, not the sustained multi-generation feedback loop where selection bias compounds into the selecting model's own training data.

The representation learning literature documents several mechanisms by which embedding spaces can lose expressiveness. \citet{jing2022understanding} characterize dimensional collapse in contrastive learning, where embeddings are driven into low-dimensional subspaces; \citet{hua2021feature} identify correlated feature axes as a driver of this collapse; and \citet{papyan2020prevalence} show that deep network representations converge to low-dimensional simplex structures during prolonged training. \citet{laurent2024feature} argue that feature collapse can be benign in classification, but our findings demonstrate that in iterative self-training, the same geometric contraction becomes pathological---it causes diversity selection to invert its intended effect.

\subsection{Representation Drift and Proxy Misalignment}

Our work connects two established literatures that, together, explain why internal-embedding diversity selection fails under iterative training.

The concept drift literature studies how learned representations degrade under sustained distribution shift. \citet{lu2019learning} and \citet{gama2014survey} provide comprehensive taxonomies of drift detection and adaptation. In the continual learning setting, \citet{caccia2022new} quantify abrupt representation change during sequential training, and \citet{davari2022probing} demonstrate that representation-level forgetting proceeds independently of task performance---paralleling our finding that embedding geometry diverges from content diversity even as standard representation quality metrics (RankMe, $k$-NN accuracy) remain stable.

The Goodhart's law and reward hacking literature formalizes the failure of proxy optimization under distribution shift. \citet{gao2023scaling} derive scaling laws showing that overoptimizing a proxy reward model degrades true objective performance; \citet{skalse2022defining} prove that non-trivial proxy rewards are inherently exploitable; \citet{pan2022effects} map how proxy-objective misalignment compounds under increasing optimization pressure; and \citet{karwowski2024goodhart} provide geometric characterizations of when proxy optimization diverges from the true objective. The embedding alignment gap is an instance of this phenomenon: internal embedding diversity serves as a proxy for content diversity, and this proxy progressively loses fidelity as the model's representations co-evolve with the selected data distribution.

Finally, measuring diversity itself requires careful metric design. Distinct-N \citep{li2016diversity} and Self-BLEU \citep{zhu2018texygen} quantify surface-level lexical diversity, while \citet{tevet2021evaluating} audit failure modes of both n-gram and neural diversity metrics. MAUVE \citep{pillutla2021mauve} measures distributional gaps between generated and human text via embedding-space divergence frontiers. We use rare n-gram density as our content diversity measure precisely because, unlike embedding-based metrics, it is model-independent and directly captures the lexical tail erosion that defines model collapse.

\paragraph{Positioning.} The embedding alignment gap as a concept---that proxy metrics degrade under optimization---is well established across the literatures surveyed above. Our contribution is not conceptual novelty but empirical quantification: we provide a controlled factorial ablation (four methods $\times$ three seeds) that decomposes the failure into its constituent factors, a diagnostic metric (selection ratio) that tracks proxy-target divergence in real time, and evidence that the failure is specific to internal embeddings rather than to diversity selection in general.

37	\subsection{RGDS Accelerates Catastrophic Perplexity Degradation}
38	\label{sec:result_c1}
39	
40	RGDS is the only method that exhibits catastrophic performance degradation across generations. At Generation~7, RGDS reaches a perplexity of $74.29 \pm 7.71$ ($n{=}3$), compared to $47.04 \pm 2.90$ for Uncurated ($n{=}3$; +58\%) and $43.18 \pm 1.43$ for Random~50\% ($n{=}3$; +72\%). All three seeds show consistent catastrophic degradation---75.07 (seed=42), 81.57 (seed=123), and 66.22 (seed=456)---with all values far exceeding the 43--47 range of the non-RGDS methods. The inter-seed variance of RGDS ($\sigma = 7.71$) substantially exceeds that of any other method ($\sigma \leq 2.97$), reflecting the stochastic dynamics of the co-degradation feedback loop.
41	
42	The selection ratio traces the mechanism behind this degradation (Figure~\ref{fig:ratio_trajectory}). RGDS's mean selection ratio follows an overall declining trend from ${\sim}1.0$ at Generation~0 to $0.64 \pm 0.20$ at Generation~7 ($n{=}3$). Seeds 42 and 123 reach deeply inverted ratios (0.52 and 0.52 respectively), while seed=456 exhibits a late-generation rebound from 0.65 at Generation~6 to 0.87 at Generation~7---without any corresponding improvement in perplexity (66.22 vs.\ 43--47 for non-RGDS methods). This dissociation between ratio recovery and perplexity indicates that once the embedding space has been sufficiently corrupted, even a partial restoration of selection alignment cannot reverse the accumulated damage to model quality. Across all seeds, RGDS preferentially retains vocabulary-poor samples relative to the full generated pool.
43	
44	\subsection{External Embeddings Avoid the Alignment Gap}
45	\label{sec:result_c2}
46	
47	External-only selection applies the identical selection algorithm and 50\% data budget but uses frozen Contriever embeddings. It avoids catastrophic degradation entirely: its Generation~7 perplexity of $46.36 \pm 2.97$ ($n{=}3$) falls within the range of Uncurated ($47.04 \pm 2.90$) and Random~50\% ($43.18 \pm 1.43$).
48	
49	External-only maintains a selection ratio above~1.0 throughout all generations ($1.16 \pm 0.08$ at Generation~7), indicating continued preferential retention of content-diverse samples.
50	
51	Since RGDS and External-only differ in exactly one variable---the embedding source---the 27.9-point perplexity gap at Generation~7 ($74.29$ vs.\ $46.36$) is directly attributable to the use of co-degrading internal representations. The selection algorithm is not at fault; the failure is specific to coupling data selection to embeddings that co-evolve with the collapsing model.
52	
53	Notably, External-only does not significantly outperform Random~50\% in perplexity ($46.36 \pm 2.97$ vs.\ $43.18 \pm 1.43$; $p = 0.198$, Welch's $t$-test, $n{=}3$). Despite maintaining a selection ratio above~1.0, the ``intelligent'' diversity signal from frozen external embeddings provides no measurable advantage over uninformed random subsampling. This null result reinforces the practical implication discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}: random sampling is a zero-cost alternative that matches the performance of embedding-guided selection when embeddings are stable and avoids the catastrophic failure when they are not.
54	
55	\subsection{Internal Selection Underperforms Random Baseline}
56	\label{sec:result_c3}
57	
58	The comparison between RGDS and Random~50\% constitutes the cleanest controlled ablation in our design. Both methods operate under identical conditions---same 50\% data budget, same training protocol, same seed infrastructure, same Generation~0 checkpoint---differing only in the selection mechanism: diversity-based curation via the model's own embeddings (RGDS) versus uninformed uniform sampling (Random~50\%). Any performance difference is therefore attributable solely to the selection mechanism, free from the data-volume confound present in comparisons against Uncurated (50\% vs.\ 100\%).
59	
60	Under this controlled comparison, RGDS exhibits catastrophically worse performance. Its Generation~7 perplexity ($74.29 \pm 7.71$, $n{=}3$) exceeds Random~50\% ($43.18 \pm 1.43$, $n{=}3$) by $+$72\% ($p = .017$, Welch's $t$, $d = 5.61$). The effect is consistent across all three seeds, with each RGDS run (75.07, 81.57, 66.22) far exceeding the non-RGDS cluster ceiling of ${\sim}47$. Internal embedding diversity selection does not merely fail to improve upon random sampling---it actively degrades model quality by a margin that dwarfs all other method differences in this study.
61	
62	Rare n-gram ratio corroborates the perplexity finding: RGDS retains $0.0061 \pm 0.0009$ at Generation~7, compared to $0.0098 \pm 0.0003$ for Random~50\%---a 38\% reduction in lexical tail content ($p = .014$, $d = -5.66$). The mechanism designed to maximize diversity produces outputs that are measurably \emph{less} diverse than those from uninformed subsampling.
63	
64	This within-budget contrast should be distinguished from the RGDS vs.\ Uncurated comparison ($+$58\%), which conflates any selection effect with a data quantity difference (50\% vs.\ 100\%). The Random~50\% vs.\ Uncurated comparison (\S\ref{sec:result_s3}) similarly involves a budget confound and does not reach significance ($p = .133$), reinforcing that the within-budget RGDS-vs.-Random ablation provides the most interpretable causal evidence for the alignment gap.
65	
66	\subsection{Random Pruning: A Directional Observation}
67	\label{sec:result_s3}
68	
69	Random~50\% ($43.18 \pm 1.43$, $n{=}3$) achieves lower Generation~7 perplexity than Uncurated ($47.04 \pm 2.90$, $n{=}3$), a reduction of 8.2\% consistent across all three seeds. However, this cross-budget comparison conflates any selection benefit with a data quantity effect (50\% vs.\ 100\%), and the difference does not reach conventional significance ($p = 0.133$, Welch's $t$-test). We report it as a directional observation rather than a confirmed finding, and draw no causal inference about budget effects from this comparison alone.
70	
71	If confirmed with additional statistical power, this result would suggest that training on a random 50\% subset provides mild regularization compared to using all generated data, consistent with observations that data pruning can improve generalization even without informed selection \citep{sorscher2022beyond}.
72	
73	While the perplexity difference remains directional, Random~50\% shows a statistically significant advantage in lexical diversity: its Generation~7 rare n-gram ratio ($0.0098 \pm 0.0003$) exceeds Uncurated ($0.0090 \pm 0.0004$) with $p = 0.025$ (two-sided $t$-test, $n{=}3$). Even uninformed subsampling preserves content diversity better than retaining all generated data, suggesting that merely reducing the volume of self-generated training data slows lexical tail erosion.
74	
75	\subsection{Lexical Diversity Collapse Across Methods}
76	\label{sec:result_diversity}
77	
78	RGDS exhibits the sharpest decline in rare token ratio, dropping from approximately 0.010 at Generation~0 to $0.0061 \pm 0.0009$ at Generation~7 (Table~\ref{tab:gen7_summary}). The remaining methods converge to a narrower band: Random~50\% ($0.0098 \pm 0.0003$), Uncurated ($0.0090 \pm 0.0004$), and External-only ($0.0102 \pm 0.0004$). Relative to the WikiText-103 baseline rare token ratio of approximately 0.029, all non-RGDS methods exhibit roughly 65\% lexical tail erosion by Generation~7; RGDS reaches approximately 80\%.
79	
80	Unlike the perplexity-level normal cluster (ANOVA $p = 0.219$; \S\ref{sec:result_c1}), the rare n-gram differences among non-RGDS methods are statistically significant (ANOVA $p = 0.007$, $n{=}3$ per method). In particular, Uncurated retains significantly fewer rare n-grams than Random~50\% ($p = 0.025$, two-sided $t$-test). Lexical diversity collapse is primarily driven by the iterative self-training loop itself \citep{shumailov2024ai}, but the degree of erosion is modulated by data selection: even uninformed curation (random subsampling) provides measurable protection relative to using all generated data. RGDS is distinctive in accelerating this inherent degradation far beyond all other methods.

116	\subsection{Representation Metrics Do Not Track Content Collapse}
117	\label{sec:result_rankme}
118	
119	RankMe values at Generation~7 are comparable across all methods (289--293; Table~\ref{tab:gen7_summary}), with no method showing a meaningfully different value ($292.54 \pm 5.91$ for RGDS vs.\ ${\sim}290$ for non-RGDS methods). 122	\label{sec:result_scaling}

124	Results from GPT2-Medium (355M) confirm that model collapse generalizes to larger models and is substantially amplified. 0	# Paper Framing — Embedding Alignment Gap
1	
2	## Target Venue
3	EMNLP 2026 ARR (deadline: May 25, 2026) — Findings full paper (8 pages)
4	
5	## Title (working)
6	"The Embedding Alignment Gap: Why Diversity-Based Data Selection Accelerates Model Collapse in Iterative Self-Training"
7	
8	## Core Insight
9	In iterative self-training (student-as-generator feedback loop), the geometric diversity of a model's internal embeddings becomes systematically misaligned with content diversity (measured by rare n-gram survival). This "alignment gap" shows an overall declining trend across generations (with a transient early rebound at Gen 1-3 before accelerating decline from Gen 4), causing diversity-based data selection using internal representations to **accelerate** rather than prevent model collapse. All methods that do not rely on degrading internal embeddings — including frozen external embeddings, random selection, and no selection — avoid this catastrophic failure mode.
10	
11	## Core Claims
12	
13	### C1: Alignment Gap Exists and Worsens Progressively
14	- Internal embedding diversity selection ratio degrades from ~1.04 (Gen 0) to ~0.52 (Gen 7)
15	- Overall declining trend with transient early rebound (Gen 1-3: 0.91→0.93→0.94) before accelerating decline from Gen 4
16	- The model increasingly selects vocabulary-poor samples when using its own representations for diversity scoring
17	- Evidence: Phase 2 RGDS selection diagnostics (GPT2-125M, WikiText-103, self-iterate)
18	
19	### C2-revised: The Failure Is Specific to Internal Embeddings (D013/D014/D015)
20	- RGDS is the **only** method showing catastrophic performance degradation
21	- {random_50, external_only, uncurated} form a "normal cluster" (gen7 PPL range: 43-50), while RGDS is a catastrophic outlier (gen7 PPL 75-82)
22	- External selection ratio stable >1.0 (1.10-1.28 across seeds); random ratio stable ~1.0 (0.96-1.06); only RGDS degrades (1.04→0.52)
23	- ⚠️ External vs uncurated ordering is **cross-seed inconsistent** (seed=42: ext wins 9.5%; seed=123: uncurated wins 7.6%) — cannot claim external > uncurated
24	- ⚠️ **D016 UPDATE**: random_50 三 seed 完成（Mean PPL=43.18±1.43）。两 seed 都显示 random < external（seed42: -5.1%, seed123: -15.9%）。差距不再是 noise——趋向 Scenario 2（random 显著优于 external）。等 seed=456 external 完成后做 3-seed t 检验定论。若确认 → 升级 claim：外部嵌入选择（ratio >1.0 过度偏好 rare-rich）也次优，保持自然分布（ratio ~1.0）是最优策略（Goodhart's Law 实例）
25	- The key insight: the problem is not "which selection method is best" but "using degrading internal representations for selection is catastrophically harmful"
26	
27	### C3: The Gap Causes Accelerated Collapse (D013 upgraded)
28	- RGDS vs random_50 (same 50% data budget): PPL 75.07 vs 43.20 (**+74%**), rare n-gram 0.0051 vs 0.0096 (**-47%**) — fully attributable to selection mechanism, data budget controlled

30	- Complete causal chain: embedding space contracts → "geometrically diverse" = "vocabulary-poor" → selection amplifies homogeneity → accelerated collapse
31	- random_50 baseline is the cleanest ablation: isolates selection quality from data budget effect

EMNLP 2026 ARR (deadline: May 25, 2026) — Findings full paper (8 pages)

## Title (working)
"The Embedding Alignment Gap: Why Diversity-Based Data Selection Accelerates Model Collapse in Iterative Self-Training"

## Core Insight
In iterative self-training (student-as-generator feedback loop), the geometric diversity of a model's internal embeddings becomes systematically misaligned with content diversity (measured by rare n-gram survival). This "alignment gap" shows an overall declining trend across generations (with a transient early rebound at Gen 1-3 before accelerating decline from Gen 4), causing diversity-based data selection using internal representations to **accelerate** rather than prevent model collapse. All methods that do not rely on degrading internal embeddings — including frozen external embeddings, random selection, and no selection — avoid this catastrophic failure mode.

## Core Claims

### C1: Alignment Gap Exists and Worsens Progressively
- Internal embedding diversity selection ratio degrades from ~1.04 (Gen 0) to ~0.52 (Gen 7)

- The model increasingly selects vocabulary-poor samples when using its own representations for diversity scoring
- Evidence: Phase 2 RGDS selection diagnostics (GPT2-125M, WikiText-103, self-iterate)

### C2-revised: The Failure Is Specific to Internal Embeddings (D013/D014/D015)
